claim: Somatosensory neurons (SSNs) that detect and transduce mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli densely innervate an animal's skin.
source: Somatosensory neurons (SSNs) that detect and transduce mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli densely innervate an animal's skin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function and distribution of somatosensory neurons.

claim: Epidermal cells provide the first point of contact for sensory stimuli.
source: However, although epidermal cells provide the first point of contact for sensory stimuli, our understanding of roles that epidermal cells play in SSN function, particularly nociception, remains limited.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about the position of epidermal cells.

claim: Stimulating Drosophila epidermal cells elicits activation of SSNs including nociceptors.
source: Here, we show that stimulating Drosophila epidermal cells elicits activation of SSNs including nociceptors and triggers a variety of behavior outputs, including avoidance and escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including calcium imaging and behavioral assays.

claim: Stimulating Drosophila epidermal cells triggers a variety of behavior outputs, including avoidance and escape.
source: Here, we show that stimulating Drosophila epidermal cells elicits activation of SSNs including nociceptors and triggers a variety of behavior outputs, including avoidance and escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic and thermogenetic experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Drosophila epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
source: Further, we find that epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive and that epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the store-operated calcium channel Orai.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data from dissociated epidermal cells and body wall preparations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the store-operated calcium channel Orai.
source: Further, we find that epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive and that epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the store-operated calcium channel Orai.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and pharmacological inhibition studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: Epidermal cell stimulation augments larval responses to acute nociceptive stimuli.
source: Epidermal cell stimulation augments larval responses to acute nociceptive stimuli and promotes prolonged hypersensitivity to subsequent mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing enhanced responses when epidermal stimulation is combined with mechanical or nociceptor stimulation, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Epidermal cell stimulation promotes prolonged hypersensitivity to subsequent mechanical stimuli.
source: Epidermal cell stimulation augments larval responses to acute nociceptive stimuli and promotes prolonged hypersensitivity to subsequent mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing sensitization lasting several minutes after epidermal stimulation, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Epidermal cells are key determinants of nociceptive sensitivity and sensitization.
source: Hence, epidermal cells are key determinants of nociceptive sensitivity and sensitization, acting as primary sensors of noxious stimuli that tune nociceptor output and drive protective behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that epidermal cells respond to mechanical stimuli and modulate nociceptor activity.

claim: Epidermal cells act as primary sensors of noxious stimuli that tune nociceptor output and drive protective behaviors.
source: Hence, epidermal cells are key determinants of nociceptive sensitivity and sensitization, acting as primary sensors of noxious stimuli that tune nociceptor output and drive protective behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing epidermal mechanosensitivity and their ability to activate nociceptors.

claim: Class IV dendrite arborization (C4da) neurons are necessary and sufficient for nociception in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, a single class of identified somatosensory neurons (SSNs), class IV dendrite arborization (C4da) neurons, are necessary and sufficient for nociception; inactivating C4da neurons renders larvae insensitive to noxious stimuli whereas activating these neurons drives nocifensive behavior responses (Hwang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2017; Burgos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Inactivating C4da neurons renders larvae insensitive to noxious stimuli.
source: In Drosophila, a single class of identified somatosensory neurons (SSNs), class IV dendrite arborization (C4da) neurons, are necessary and sufficient for nociception; inactivating C4da neurons renders larvae insensitive to noxious stimuli whereas activating these neurons drives nocifensive behavior responses (Hwang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2017; Burgos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activating C4da neurons drives nocifensive behavior responses.
source: In Drosophila, a single class of identified somatosensory neurons (SSNs), class IV dendrite arborization (C4da) neurons, are necessary and sufficient for nociception; inactivating C4da neurons renders larvae insensitive to noxious stimuli whereas activating these neurons drives nocifensive behavior responses (Hwang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2017; Burgos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: UV irradiation and chemical toxins induce long-lasting allodynia and hyperalgesia in Drosophila.
source: A variety of agents that cause tissue damage including UV irradiation and chemical toxins induce long-lasting allodynia and hyperalgesia (Babcock et al., 2009; Boiko et al., 2017), but this damage-induced hypersensitivity develops on a timescale of hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Damage-induced hypersensitivity in Drosophila develops on a timescale of hours.
source: A variety of agents that cause tissue damage including UV irradiation and chemical toxins induce long-lasting allodynia and hyperalgesia (Babcock et al., 2009; Boiko et al., 2017), but this damage-induced hypersensitivity develops on a timescale of hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Drosophila display acute hypersensitivity to noxious mechanical stimuli.
source: Drosophila also display acute hypersensitivity noxious mechanical stimuli (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal Merkel cells are mechanosensory cells that signal to sensory neurons to mediate touch transduction.
source: For example, epidermal Merkel cells are mechanosensory cells that signal to sensory neurons to mediate touch transduction (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Keratinocytes are directly activated by noxious thermal and mechanical stimuli.
source: Similarly, keratinocytes are directly activated by noxious thermal and mechanical stimuli and release molecules that modulate nociceptor functions (Chung et al., 2004; Koizumi et al., 2004; Moqrich et al., 2005; Mandadi et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2019; Sadler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Keratinocytes release molecules that modulate nociceptor functions.
source: Similarly, keratinocytes are directly activated by noxious thermal and mechanical stimuli and release molecules that modulate nociceptor functions (Chung et al., 2004; Koizumi et al., 2004; Moqrich et al., 2005; Mandadi et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2019; Sadler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal cells in invertebrates and vertebrates ensheathe nociceptors in mesaxon-like structures.
source: Furthermore, epidermal cells in invertebrates and vertebrates ensheathe nociceptors in mesaxon-like structures (Cauna, 1973; Chalfie and Sulston, 1981; Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012b; O'Brien et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2019), and these sheaths may serve as sites of epidermis-nociceptor signaling (Yin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal sheaths may serve as sites of epidermis-nociceptor signaling.
source: Furthermore, epidermal cells in invertebrates and vertebrates ensheathe nociceptors in mesaxon-like structures (Cauna, 1973; Chalfie and Sulston, 1981; Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012b; O'Brien et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2019), and these sheaths may serve as sites of epidermis-nociceptor signaling (Yin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Epidermal ensheathment is required for normal responses to noxious mechanical stimuli in Drosophila.
source: Indeed, epidermal ensheathment is required for normal responses to noxious mechanical stimuli in Drosophila (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetic activation of nociceptive C4da neurons triggered nocifensive behaviors including c-bending and rolling in 100% of larvae.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Hwang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2017), C4da activation triggered nocifensive behaviors including c-bending and rolling in 100% of larvae (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells elicited nocifensive c-bending and/or rolling behaviors in 73% of larvae.
source: We found that optogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells, like C4da neurons, elicited nocifensive c-bending and/or rolling behaviors in 73% of larvae (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), without significantly altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells does not significantly alter nociceptor morphogenesis.
source: We found that optogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells, like C4da neurons, elicited nocifensive c-bending and/or rolling behaviors in 73% of larvae (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), without significantly altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Muscle stimulation triggered hunching behavior followed by prolonged freezing.
source: In contrast, stimulation of other body wall cell types elicited a variety of non-nociceptive behavior outputs: e.g., muscle stimulation triggered hunching behavior followed by prolonged freezing, whereas glia stimulation reproducibly induced only hunching behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–I; Zimmermann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–I.

claim: Glia stimulation reproducibly induced only hunching behavior.
source: In contrast, stimulation of other body wall cell types elicited a variety of non-nociceptive behavior outputs: e.g., muscle stimulation triggered hunching behavior followed by prolonged freezing, whereas glia stimulation reproducibly induced only hunching behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–I; Zimmermann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–I.

claim: Epidermal cells are the only non-neuronal body wall cell type that triggers robust nocifensive behavioral responses.
source: Thus, epidermal cells are the only non-neuronal body wall cell type that triggers robust nocifensive behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the optogenetic screen data comparing different body wall cell types.

claim: All epidermal drivers except for sr-GAL4 elicited rolling responses.
source: All epidermal drivers except for sr-GAL4, which is expressed in apodemes but no other epidermal cells, elicited rolling responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: sr-GAL4 is expressed in apodemes but no other epidermal cells.
source: All epidermal drivers except for sr-GAL4, which is expressed in apodemes but no other epidermal cells, elicited rolling responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the expression pattern of a GAL4 driver line.

claim: More than 75% of larvae expressing TRPA1 in all nociceptors exhibited rolling behavior in response to a thermal stimulus.
source: In contrast, we found that >75% of larvae expressing TRPA1 in all nociceptors exhibited rolling behavior in response to a thermal stimulus (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of epidermal cells induced robust rolling responses in >75% of larvae.
source: Likewise, thermogenetic activation of epidermal cells induced robust rolling responses in >75% of larvae, and addition of GAL80 transgenes (tsh-GAL80 elav-GAL80) that silenced the sparse R38F11-GAL4 VNC expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) had no effect on the rolling frequency (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Addition of GAL80 transgenes (tsh-GAL80 elav-GAL80) that silenced the sparse R38F11-GAL4 VNC expression had no effect on the rolling frequency.
source: Likewise, thermogenetic activation of epidermal cells induced robust rolling responses in >75% of larvae, and addition of GAL80 transgenes (tsh-GAL80 elav-GAL80) that silenced the sparse R38F11-GAL4 VNC expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) had no effect on the rolling frequency (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and 5.

claim: Sparse thermogenetic activation of nociceptors (<5 cells) yielded no significant increase in nocifensive rolling.
source: Of note, prior studies demonstrated that sparse thermogenetic activation of nociceptors (<5 cells) yielded no significant increase in nocifensive rolling whereas activation of >10 cells was required to elicit rolling responses in a majority of larvae (Robertson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Activation of >10 nociceptor cells was required to elicit rolling responses in a majority of larvae.
source: Of note, prior studies demonstrated that sparse thermogenetic activation of nociceptors (<5 cells) yielded no significant increase in nocifensive rolling whereas activation of >10 cells was required to elicit rolling responses in a majority of larvae (Robertson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal stimulation likely engages numerous C4da neurons to elicit behavioral responses.
source: Hence, epidermal stimulation likely engages numerous C4da neurons to elicit these behavioral responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work showing that multiple nociceptors must be activated to elicit rolling.

claim: The epidermis is innervated by C3da, chordotonal (Cho) neurons, and proprioceptive C1da neurons in addition to C4da nociceptors.
source: In addition to C4da nociceptors, the epidermis is innervated by a variety of other SSNs including mechanosensory C3da and chordotonal (Cho) neurons and proprioceptive C1da neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about Drosophila sensory neurons.

claim: Direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs.
source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching.
source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Freezing and hunching behaviors are associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons.
source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal cells may broadly modulate SSN activity in Drosophila.
source: These data suggest that epidermal cells may broadly modulate SSN activity in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that epidermal stimulation elicits behaviors associated with multiple SSN types.

claim: Only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior when stimulated.
source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claim: Stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing.
source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claim: Stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses.
source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claim: Optogenetic epidermal stimulation elicited all behaviors observed with SSN stimulation, with nocifensive behaviors (c-bending, rolling) predominating initially, followed by non-nociceptive behaviors (backing, freezing).
source: In contrast, optogenetic epidermal stimulation elicited all of these behaviors, with nocifensive behaviors (c-bending, rolling) predominating initially, followed by non-nociceptive behaviors (backing, freezing) (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: Latency to rolling was significantly longer following epidermal stimulation compared to stimulation of C4da.
source: First, although rapid, latency to rolling was significantly longer following epidermal stimulation compared to stimulation of C4da (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The duration of rolling, bending, and backing responses was significantly longer for epidermis versus SSN stimulation.
source: Second, the duration of rolling, bending, and backing responses was significantly longer for epidermis versus SSN stimulation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Backing and freezing behaviors persisted beyond the duration of the light stimulus for epidermis but not SSN stimulation.
source: Third, backing and freezing behaviors persisted beyond the duration of the light stimulus for epidermis but not SSN stimulation (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Epidermal stimulation triggers more robust, varied, and prolonged behaviors compared to responses from direct stimulation of discrete SSN subtypes.
source: In summary, we find that epidermal stimulation triggers more robust, varied, and prolonged behaviors compared to responses from direct stimulation of discrete SSN subtypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral comparison data.

claim: Epidermal stimulation triggered rapid and robust calcium transients in nociceptive C4da neurons.
source: We found that epidermal stimulation triggered rapid and robust calcium transients in nociceptive C4da neurons, responses that were not observed in the absence of ATR or in effector-only controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Epidermal stimulation evoked calcium transients in mechanosensory C3da and Cho neurons, and in proprioceptive C1da neurons.
source: Epidermal stimulation likewise evoked calcium transients in mechanosensory C3da and Cho neurons, and in proprioceptive C1da neurons (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C–E.

claim: Epidermal stimulation can broadly modulate activity of larval SSNs.
source: Hence, epidermal stimulation can broadly modulate activity of larval SSNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the calcium imaging data showing responses in multiple SSN types.

claim: Inhibiting C4da or C3da+Cho neurotransmission significantly reduced the frequency and duration of epidermal-evoked rolling and backing behaviors, respectively.
source: We found that inhibiting C4da or C3da+Cho neurotransmission significantly reduced the frequency and duration of epidermal-evoked rolling and backing behaviors, respectively (Figure 3F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using tetanus toxin to block neurotransmitter release, shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: C4da and C3da/Cho neurons act downstream of epidermal cells to drive behaviors.
source: These data suggest that C4da and C3da/Cho neurons act downstream of epidermal cells to drive behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the neurotransmitter release blocking experiments.

claim: TnT expression in C4da neurons did not completely block epidermis-evoked nocifensive behaviors.
source: We note that TnT expression in C4da neurons did not completely block epidermis-evoked nocifensive behaviors, and this likely reflects both incomplete C4da neuron silencing and epidermal activation of other SSNs that promote nociceptive outputs including C3da neurons, C2da neurons, and Cho neurons (Ohyama et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2017; Burgos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an inference about the underlying mechanisms.

claim: Silencing C4da or C3da/Cho neurons while stimulating epidermal cells led to an increase in the non-nocifensive behaviors hunching and freezing.
source: Further, silencing C4da or C3da/Cho neurons while stimulating epidermal cells led to an increase in the non-nocifensive behaviors hunching and freezing (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The nervous system prioritizes nocifensive behavioral outputs following epidermal stimulation.
source: These results, along with the observation that rolling behaviors predominate the early behavioral responses to epidermal stimulation (Figure 2B), suggest that the nervous system prioritizes nocifensive behavioral outputs following epidermal stimulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the behavioral data.

claim: Epidermal cells and SSNs are functionally coupled.
source: These data support a model in which epidermal cells and SSNs are functionally coupled.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing that epidermal stimulation activates SSNs and drives behaviors.

claim: Simultaneous epidermal and C4da stimulation significantly enhanced the magnitude and duration of calcium responses in C4da axons.
source: Simultaneous stimulation significantly enhanced the magnitude and duration of calcium responses in C4da axons (Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae.
source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Selective stimulation of C4da neurons induced rolling in 63% of larvae.
source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Selective stimulation of epidermal cells induced rolling in 18% of larvae.
source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Simultaneous stimulation elicited a significantly higher number of rolls among responders than stimulation of nociceptors or epidermal cells alone.
source: Furthermore, simultaneous stimulation elicited a significantly higher number of rolls among responders than stimulation of nociceptors or epidermal cells alone (26.9 rolls for C4da+Epi, 4.9 for C4da, and 5.3 for Epi stimulation; Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll.
source: Likewise, simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll (Figure 4I) and increased the duration of rolling behaviors (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Simultaneous stimulation increased the duration of rolling behaviors.
source: Likewise, simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll (Figure 4I) and increased the duration of rolling behaviors (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Concurrent epidermal stimulation significantly increased touch-evoked nocifensive responses, yielding a 91% or 49% increase in rolling responses to 20 mN or 50 mN von Frey stimulus, respectively.
source: This concurrent epidermal stimulation significantly increased touch-evoked nocifensive responses, yielding a 91% or 49% increase in rolling responses to 20 mN or 50 mN von Frey stimulus, respectively (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: dTRPA1-mediated epidermal stimulation significantly sensitized larvae to a subsequent mechanical stimulus, increasing the roll probability more than twofold.
source: Indeed, we found that dTRPA1-mediated epidermal stimulation significantly sensitized larvae to a subsequent mechanical stimulus, increasing the roll probability more than twofold.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: dTRPA1-mediated stimulation of C4da neurons did not induce mechanical sensitization.
source: In contrast, dTRPA1-mediated stimulation of C4da neurons did not induce mechanical sensitization, and we confirmed this result with two independent C4da neuron drivers (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Activation of epidermal cells but not C4da nociceptors alone induces prolonged sensitization to noxious mechanical stimuli.
source: Thus, activation of epidermal cells but not C4da nociceptors alone induces prolonged sensitization to noxious mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral data comparing epidermal and nociceptor stimulation.

claim: Thermogenetic epidermal stimulation yielded persistent sensitization that recovered over a timescale of minutes (τ=337 s).
source: Thermogenetic epidermal stimulation yielded persistent sensitization that recovered over a timescale of minutes (τ=337 s, Figure 4M and N).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4M and N.

claim: The magnitude and duration of mechanical sensitization by thermogenetic epidermal stimulation was remarkably similar to sensitization evoked by a prior mechanical stimulus (63% roll probability in response to a second stimulus, τ=334 s).
source: The magnitude and duration of mechanical sensitization by thermogenetic epidermal stimulation was remarkably similar to sensitization evoked by a prior mechanical stimulus (63% roll probability in response to a second stimulus, τ=334 s, Figure 4N, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Epidermal cells are mechanosensitive cells that signal to SSNs to drive acute nocifensive behaviors and prolong mechanical sensitization.
source: Altogether our data support a model whereby epidermal cells are mechanosensitive cells that signal to SSNs to drive acute nocifensive behaviors and prolong mechanical sensitization.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Vertebrate epidermal cells directly respond to mechanical stimuli.
source: Prior studies have shown that vertebrate epidermal cells directly respond to mechanical stimuli (Koizumi et al., 2004; Haeberle et al., 2008; Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Radial stretch elicits calcium responses in epidermal cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that radial stretch elicits calcium responses in epidermal cells in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data from dissociated epidermal cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: A low 0.5% stretch activated 18% of cells and a subsequent 1% stretch recruited an additional 10% of stretch-responding cells.
source: For example, a low 0.5% stretch activated 18% of cells and a subsequent 1% stretch recruited an additional 10% of stretch-responding cells (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: 51% of epidermal cells displayed stretch sensitivity.
source: Overall, 51% of epidermal cells displayed stretch sensitivity (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge.
source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 35% of epidermal cells responded to laminar flow.
source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow.
source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 50% of epidermal cells exhibited a robust calcium transient in response to a 25 μm membrane displacement using a glass probe.
source: We found that 50% of epidermal cells exhibited a robust calcium transient in response to a 25 μm membrane displacement using a glass probe (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the calcium imaging data from dissociated and semi-intact preparations.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of acutely dissociated epidermal cells revealed expression of more than 20 cation channels, including the mechanosensitive ion channels Piezo, TMEM63, and TMCO.
source: RNA-seq analysis of acutely dissociated epidermal cells revealed expression of more than 20 cation channels, including the mechanosensitive ion channels Piezo, TMEM63, and TMCO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Orai blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus.
source: Our behavioral screen identified one channel, Orai, the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel (Feske et al., 2006), that blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) or altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Orai is the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel.
source: Our behavioral screen identified one channel, Orai, the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel (Feske et al., 2006), that blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) or altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Task6 is an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels.
source: Interestingly, our screen uncovered an epidermal role for Task6, an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels (Fink et al., 1996), in mechanonociception, as Task6 RNAi increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Task6 RNAi increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus.
